**1. The idea.** The animation shows that the same income check can buy very different amounts depending on when you retire. Three illustrative retirees, Edna, Carl and Ruth, each get a check that rises 2% a year. They start in different months: Jan 1949, Jan 1966 and Aug 2006. The animation uses US consumer prices (CPI-U) to count how many crates of goods each check buys.

**2. What changes.** In frames 1 and 2, the three rows of crates look about equal. By frame 3, which is labeled "crates at year 20", the rows have diverged. Edna's row is still full, Ruth's is nearly full, and Carl's has shrunk a lot. Frames 4 to 6 add the totals. Edna can buy 10 crates, Carl about 4 and Ruth about 9. The timeline underneath shows each person's start month.

**3. What it means.** A check that grows 2% a year only holds its buying power if actual inflation stays at or below about 2%. Carl started in 1966, just before a long stretch of high inflation. His check lost more than half its real value over 20 years. Edna and Ruth started in calmer periods and kept most or all of theirs. The outcome depends heavily on when you start, which you can't control. The caption says "US only · history, not a forecast" and every name is tagged "ILLUSTRATIVE". So these are example cases from past data, not a prediction.

**4. Advice a viewer might take.** The takeaway is that a fixed payment, or one with a small fixed raise, carries inflation risk over a long retirement. When you compare payout options, look at whether the payments adjust for actual inflation or only rise by a set percentage. Also consider how much of your spending that income has to cover. The animation doesn't say which option is better, and it doesn't give the cost of inflation protection, which usually means a lower starting payment. It also can't say what inflation will do in the future. A viewer should treat it as a reason to ask that question, not as a rule.
